title: DeCovarT reproducibility
text:
This book is the narrative companion to scripts/. Computation stays in the scripts; the chapters are theory, design, and criticism of how those scripts should be run.
The scientific target is DeCovarT’s cell-type Gaussians: sparse precisions \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}\equiv\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1} and means \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}, estimated from labelled single-cell transcriptomes and plugged into the bulk convolution. Indices follow the article Methods: gene g=1,\ldots,G, cell type j=1,\ldots,J, sample i=1,\ldots,N.
The planned Suppinger benchmark is a 3\times 2\times 2 product, not a single pipeline. Three sparse-precision estimators (huge graphical lasso, SILGGM after a nonparanormal map, and PLNnetwork), two lifts from cells to a population Gaussian, and two gene-panel strategies (the naive screen alone, or that screen plus an optional stricter Pareto refinement). That is 12 routes. The aim is to see which steps move deconvolution, not to retain every cell of the product in the paper. Bures–Wasserstein alignment, GmGM, and sparse-plus-low-rank GGMs stay perspectives; they are not factors in Figure 1.

title: 3  Naive gene screen
text:
3.1 Building \mathcal{G}_{0}
This chapter builds a working universe \mathcal{G}_{0} on which a GGM can be estimated. Genes are scored from one labelled single-cell reference, used as a signature, not from a multi-sample atlas. Global ranks (highly variable genes) and a short knowledge-driven marker list both remove genes from the whole transcriptome. The all-versus-all refinement that uses \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} comes after GRN inference (Section 7.1).
Notation: gene g=1,\ldots,G; cell type j=1,\ldots,J; cell c=1,\ldots,C. A cell labelled as type j is written c_{j}. Bulk samples stay indexed by i, as in the article. The DeCovarT convolution is linear in \boldsymbol{p} only on an additive scale (Note 3.1).

title: 3  Naive gene screen
text:
Important 3.1: :warning: Keep the mixture on a linear scale



The convolution \boldsymbol{y}\mid(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p})\sim\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p},\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) is linear in \boldsymbol{p} only if \boldsymbol{\mu} and \boldsymbol{y} live on the same additive scale (counts, CPM, or TPM). Logarithms, SCTransform Pearson residuals, and nonparanormal scores break that map (Sturm et al. 2019; Jin and Liu 2021; Hoffmann et al. 2006). Use residualisation only to rank genes; export DeCovarT moments on the linear scale. The probabilistic reason is Jensen’s inequality (Note 4.2, Note 4.1).

title: 3  Naive gene screen
section: 3.2 Highly variable genes as a signal-to-noise rank
text:
3.2 Highly variable genes as a signal-to-noise rank
Single-cell UMI tables mix depth noise with biological heterogeneity. Regularised negative-binomial regression in sctransform (Hafemeister et al. 2025) / Seurat::SCTransform separates the two via Pearson residuals (Hafemeister and Satija 2019). We use that transform only to rank genes, not to normalise the table that enters glasso or PLN, and not as a factorial arm of the GRN design (Section 4.2).
On this single-cell reference the only technical covariate we actually have is library size. There is a single scRNA-seq resource, so batch, donor and unmeasured technical branches cannot be identified (Hafemeister and Satija 2019). The technical null is therefore

\log\mu_{cg}
=
\beta_{0g}
+
\operatorname{offset}(\log L_{c}),
\qquad
y_{cg}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{cg},\theta_{g}),
\tag{3.1}
with L_{c} the library size of cell c. Do not put cell type j in this null: that would remove the between-type signal the panel is meant to keep.
Pearson residuals are

r_{cg}
=
\frac{y_{cg}-\hat{\mu}_{cg}}
{\sqrt{\hat{\mu}_{cg}+\hat{\mu}_{cg}^{2}/\hat{\theta}_{g}}}.
\tag{3.2}
Figure 3.2 recalls the NB mean–variance relation and the residual scale used by SCTransform.






Figure 3.2: SCTransform negative-binomial mean–variance relation and Pearson residuals (Seurat v5).




3.2.1 Total, biological, and technical pieces
For gene g write V_{\mathrm{total},g}=\mathrm{Var}_{c}(r_{cg}) for residual variation after the depth null. That leftover is not pure biology: it still contains model misspecification. What we can split with the labels j is biological variation between versus within cell types,

\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
C_{j}
\bigl(\bar{r}_{gj}-\bar{r}_{g}\bigr)^{2},
\qquad
\bar{r}_{gj}
=
C_{j}^{-1}\sum_{c_{j}}r_{c_{j}g},\\
\mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{within},g}
&=
\sum_{j=1}^{J}
\sum_{c_{j}}
\bigl(r_{c_{j}g}-\bar{r}_{gj}\bigr)^{2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.3}
C_{j} is the number of cells labelled j. Because the residuals are globally approximately centred, \bar{r}_{g}\approx 0 and \mathrm{SS}_{\mathrm{between},g}\approx\sum_{j}C_{j}\bar{r}_{gj}^{2}. A lineage marker (high between-type, low within-type) is the gene we want. A stress-response gene (low between-type, high within-type) is not, even if its total residual variance is large. Figure 3.3 sketches that split.






Figure 3.3: Technical variation absorbed by a library-size negative-binomial null, and biological residual variation split into between-type and within-type pieces.

flowchart TD
  Y["y_cg"] --> N["NB technical null: offset log L_c only"]
  N --> R["Pearson r_cg"]
  R --> T["Total residual variance"]
  T --> B["Between type"]
  T --> W["Within type"]
  B --> S["Keep high between, low within"]
  W --> S




Figure 3.4: Residual variance after a library-size NB null. Technical variation is whatever the null absorbed; leftover variation is split into between-type and within-type biological pieces. Rank genes by a high between / low within ratio, not by total residual variance alone.





There is no calibrated differential-expression p-value here: one technical replicate cannot support DESeq2 (Note 3.4). The between-type sum of squares is a ranking score.
Use Seurat::SCTransform() with Pearson residuals (vst.flavor = "v2"). That is the residual transformation used to rank genes (Note 3.2).
After SCTransform, pull the residual matrix and compute Equation 3.3 by the labelled type j. Keep on the order of 2{,}000 genes in \mathcal{G}_{0} before any GGM (Friedman et al. 2008).

# Sketch: Pearson residuals for ranking only; export counts to the GGM.
sct <- Seurat::SCTransform(
  seu,
  method = "glmGamPoi",
  residual.feature = NULL,
  return.only.var.genes = FALSE,
  vst.flavor = "v2"
)
R <- Seurat::GetAssayData(sct, assay = "SCT", layer = "scale.data")
# rows gene g, columns cell c; align with cell-type factor j
j <- sct$celltype
ss_between <- apply(R, 1, function(r) {
  means <- tapply(r, j, mean)
  n_j <- tapply(r, j, length)
  sum(n_j * means^2)
})
ss_within <- apply(R, 1, function(r) {
  sum(tapply(r, j, function(z) sum((z - mean(z))^2)))
})
snr <- ss_between / pmax(ss_within, .Machine$double.eps)







Note 3.2: :information_source: vst.flavor = "v2" still returns Pearson residuals



Both flavours of SCTransform assume Y_{cg}\sim\mathrm{NB}(\mu_{cg},\theta_{g}) and store Pearson residuals. What changes is the fit that produces \hat\mu_{cg} and \hat\theta_{g} (Figure 3.5).
In v1 the depth slope is a gene-wise coefficient,

\log\mu_{cg}=\beta_{0g}+\beta_{1g}\log_{10}(n_{c}).

In v2 that slope is fixed at \ln 10, so library size is an offset (Choudhary and Satija 2022; Lause et al. 2021):

\log\mu_{cg}=\beta_{0g}+\log n_{c},
\qquad
\mu_{cg}=e^{\beta_{0g}}\,n_{c}.

Doubling the UMI depth then doubles every gene’s expected count. v2 also regularises dispersions with the glmGamPoi offset route, treats genes with no evidence of overdispersion as Poisson (\theta_{g}=\infty), and floors the Pearson denominator at a minimum variance (min_variance = "umi_median") before the separate residual clip. The ranking above uses those v2 residuals; it does not use Seurat’s variable-feature shortlist.






Figure 3.5: Shared negative-binomial model, and the v1 gene-wise depth slope versus the v2 offset.











Note 3.3: :information_source: HVGs are not a GGM input



Pearson residuals are closer to homoscedastic than raw UMI counts, which is why they are popular before PCA. They are still a nonlinear residualisation. Feeding them indiscriminately into SILGGM silently changes the estimand of \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} away from the latent Gaussian that DeCovarT wants at the population level. If a Gaussian GGM is used, prefer a copula / nonparanormal map on the same gene set (Section 4.3.2), or better a Poisson-lognormal latent Gaussian (Section 4.3.3).

title: 3  Naive gene screen
text:
3.3 Marker genes
Shannon entropy and Gini of relative means are compaction scores for long one-versus-rest lists. Definitions live in the DeCovarT vignette supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd.
On this reference the marker list is knowledge-driven and already short. It is stored as
data/dictionaries/mouse_gastruloid_signaling_markers.csv
with three columns: cell_type_excel (lineage name on the signalling map), cell_type_suppinger (the matching Suppinger label, or NA when that lineage is absent), and gene_marker. Because the list is a curated biological seed rather than a concatenated differential-expression shortlist, it does not by itself inflate collinearity of \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}. Seeds may later be grown by Markov boundaries (Section A.1).

title: 3  Naive gene screen
section: 3.4 Differential expression — only with biological replication
text:
3.4 Differential expression — only with biological replication
DESeq2, edgeR and limma–voom remain the workhorses of one-versus-rest ranking (Love et al. 2014). That logic does not transfer to GSE229513 as a DE experiment.






Warning 3.4: :warning: Technical pseudo-bulks are not biological replicates



Cells from a common experimental unit are not independent biological replicates. Splitting or bootstrapping cells characterises technical / sampling variability; it does not manufacture between-organoid uncertainty. Treating cells, or random partitions of cells, as DESeq2 replicates inflates apparent degrees of freedom and produces false discoveries (Squair et al. 2021; Crowell et al. 2020).
Use DESeq2 in this book only if independent biological replicates exist. For GSE229513, skip calibrated DE p-values. Rank genes by Equation 3.3 or by the knowledge table, not by a nested-model F treated as a p-value.
Bulk HTSeq tables (GSE229386) do have three biological replicates per time and Wnt schedule (Section 2.1). Those replicates support bulk DE of treatments, not cell-type GRNs from the scRNA-seq object.

title: 3  Naive gene screen
text:
3.6 Perspectives: differential networks
These methods are not in the naive screen. They need graphs, so they nominate extras for \mathcal{G}_{0} after a first GGM pass. Full algebraic detail of INDEED and D-trace lives in DeCovarT vignettes/supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd. Separation language (directed versus undirected) is in Section A.1.

3.6.1 Comparing supports, or estimating the difference
DeCovarT benefits from rewiring between populations. A gene that changes neighbourhood in \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} is a better candidate than a gene that is merely highly variable.
Fit every \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}, then compare supports. Independent glasso / SILGGM fits (Section 4.3.2) yield per-type edges; the symmetric difference of supports ranks genes by differential connectivity. The difference of two biased estimators is not a debiased estimator of \Delta_{j\ell}=\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}-\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\ell}.
Estimate \Delta_{j\ell} directly. D-trace methods target the difference of precisions without necessarily reconstructing both graphs first. Zhang and Zou (Zhang and Zou 2014) introduced the lasso-penalised D-trace loss for a single sparse precision; the differential-network extension (Yuan et al. 2017) estimates \Delta_{j\ell}. Empirically, D-trace is competitive when the difference is sparser than either graph (Plaksienko et al. 2025). It still does not produce a pair of SPD precisions. A workable proposal is: use D-trace to nominate rewiring genes, then estimate each \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} on that panel with a method from Section 4.4.


3.6.2 INDEED
INDEED multiplies a DE p-value by a permutation-filtered change in partial correlation (Zuo et al. 2016). On this reference the DE p-value assumes biological replication (Note 3.4), and the permutation null among cells of one gastruloid is a technical null. Use it, if at all, as a ranking heuristic with p_{g}^{\mathrm{DE}} replaced by a fold-change or between-type score.


3.6.3 Markov boundaries
Once a GGM exists, seeds (markers, high signal-to-noise genes, D-trace hits) can be grown by undirected neighbours \{g':\theta_{gg'}\neq 0\}. On a minimal undirected I-map that neighbour set is the Markov boundary, the smallest Markov blanket (Pearl 1988; Koller and Friedman 2009). That is undirected separation, not DAG d-separation (Section A.1, Figure A.1).

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
text:
4.1 Scope of the core pipeline
DeCovarT needs one sparse Gaussian graphical model per cell type at the population (pseudo-bulk) level, not a per-cell precision and not a directed regulatory DAG. The estimand, aligned with the article, is
\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\,\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}\bigr),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}
\equiv
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}^{-1}
\ \text{sparse},
\tag{4.1}
with undirected edges encoding conditional dependence (Friedman et al. 2008; Mazumder and Hastie 2011). Single-cell UMI profiles are the only observations.
They are not the objects that enter the deconvolution likelihood: we use them to estimate (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}) for labelled types in the Suppinger murine gastruloid resource (Suppinger et al. 2023). Downstream, those parameters discriminate types via mean shifts and precision rewiring, then enter the convolution
\boldsymbol{y}_{\cdot i}
\mid
(\boldsymbol{\zeta},\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i})
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}\!\bigl(
\boldsymbol{\mu}\,\boldsymbol{p}_{\cdot i},\,
\textstyle\sum_{j}p_{ji}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}
\bigr).
\tag{4.2}
In scope: undirected sparse precisions; single-cell transcriptomics only; stationarity; labelled cell types. The three estimators in Figure 1 are huge (graphical lasso), SILGGM after a nonparanormal map with global FDR, and PLNnetwork.
Dataset constraint. GSE229513 is a 10x Chromium 3′ v3 UMI resource with one technical scRNA-seq experiment, not independent biological replicates for GRNs (Suppinger et al. 2023). GSE250136 is a later stem-embryo dataset; it is external validation, not extra Suppinger replicates. Technical bootstrap of cells is allowed (Section 5.5); biological bootstrap is not. Networks are fit independently at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (Section 2.1).

title: 4  Undirected GGMs from single-cell transcriptomics
section: 4.2 How each estimator sees the counts
text:
4.2 How each estimator sees the counts
A transformation belongs to one estimator. It is not crossed with the other two.








Estimator
What is passed in
Object exported




huge
Continuous Gaussian table
Sparse \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}


SILGGM
Nonparanormal scores, then global FDR
Support, then an SPD refit


PLNnetwork
Raw UMI counts and a library-size offset
Latent Gaussian precision



SCTransform Pearson residuals stay in the HVG ranking of Section 3.2. Do not pass them to PLNnetwork: the PLN already has a Poisson sampling layer. Do not run the nonparanormal map before huge or before PLN; it is part of the SILGGM branch only.






Warning 4.1: :warning: Nonparanormal maps are not affine, so they break moments



huge::huge.npn() replaces each margin by a (truncated or shrunk) inverse-normal score (Liu et al. 2009). That map \varphi is monotone but not affine. Jensen’s inequality then says \varphi(\mathbb{E}[y_{g}])\neq\mathbb{E}[\varphi(y_{g})] unless the margin is degenerate (Note 4.2). A precision fitted after NPN therefore targets a different random vector from the population Gaussian DeCovarT convolves. Use NPN only inside the SILGGM branch, and never export NPN-scale means as \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j}.








Important 4.2: :warning: Transforming the response is usually the wrong GLM



DeCovarT’s mean map \boldsymbol{y}=\boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p} is additive on the measurement scale of \boldsymbol{y}. Replacing \boldsymbol{y} by \varphi(\boldsymbol{y}) and then treating the transform as Gaussian does three separate kinds of damage.
1. Jensen: moments of \varphi(\boldsymbol{y}) are not \varphi of the moments. For a convex \varphi, the probabilistic form of Jensen’s inequality states \varphi(\mathbb{E}[\boldsymbol{y}])\le\mathbb{E}[\varphi(\boldsymbol{y})], with equality iff \boldsymbol{y} is almost surely constant or \varphi is affine (Wikipedia, probabilistic form). The logarithm is concave, so

\mathbb{E}[\log y_{g}]
\le
\log\mathbb{E}[y_{g}],
\tag{4.3}
and \log1p is likewise concave on [0,\infty). A graphical lasso fitted to \log1p counts therefore targets a precision of a different random vector. The mean of the transformed table is not the transform of the mean that DeCovarT needs in Equation 4.2. Population aggregation (Section 5.3) compounds the error: the sum of transformed cells is not the transform of the sum.
2. The estimand of a transformed linear model is not the estimand of the original mean. In a Gaussian linear model, \mathbb{E}[\log y\mid x]=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}x describes multiplicative effects on y after exponentiation, not additive shifts of \mathbb{E}[y\mid x] (University of Virginia Library, interpreting log transformations). DeCovarT’s target is a linear mixture of means plus a quadratic mixture of covariances.
3. A GLM with the right mean–variance function is preferable to transforming y. Transforming the response to force Gaussianity changes the parameter. The constructive alternative on counts is the Poisson-lognormal model (Section 4.3.3), not log1p followed by graphical lasso.

text:
4.3 Three sparse-precision estimators

4.3.1 Graphical lasso in huge
huge is the maintained implementation of the graphical lasso of Friedman, Hastie and Tibshirani (Friedman et al. 2008; Mazumder and Hastie 2011; Zhao et al. 2012, 2022): a regularisation path, EBIC or StARS selection, and sparse-matrix output. The programme is the Friedman graphical lasso.

Generative model
Cells of one labelled type, at one time, are treated as independent Gaussian replicates. The precision is sparse.






%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TB
  subgraph plateC["c = 1, ..., n_j"]
    direction TB
    mu["mu_j"] --> x(("x_c"))
    Sig["Sigma_j"] --> x
  end
  Th["Theta_j = Sigma_j inverse, sparse"] --> Sig
  classDef param fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef latent fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  class mu,Sig,Th param
  class x latent




Figure 4.2: Graphical lasso generative model: independent Gaussian cells of one type, with a sparse precision.







Objective and assumptions
Let S be the sample covariance of the n cells on the gene panel. The estimator is

\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}
=
\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\Theta}\succ 0}
\Bigl[
-\log\det\boldsymbol{\Theta}
+
\operatorname{tr}(S\boldsymbol{\Theta})
+
\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\Theta}\|_{1}
\Bigr].
\tag{4.4}
Assumptions: multivariate Gaussian observations; conditional independence encoded by zeros of \boldsymbol{\Theta}; cells independent within the type-time subset; G may exceed n.


Optimisation and the \ell_{1} penalty
huge(method = "glasso") solves Equation 4.4 by graphical-lasso coordinate descent. The \ell_{1} term drives off-diagonal entries to zero. The diagonal is left unpenalised, so variances are not shrunk toward zero. A path of \lambda values is computed; one \lambda is then chosen.


Hyperparameters

\lambda path, and the selection rule in huge.select() (ebic (Foygel and Drton 2010) or stars);
whether the diagonal is penalised (default in this design: no);
the gene panel \mathcal{G}_{0} and the type-time subset.




4.3.2 SILGGM after a nonparanormal map
SILGGM tests entries of a Gaussian precision and controls FDR on the whole graph (Zhang et al. 2018a, 2018b). The arm used here is: nonparanormal scores, then de-sparsified graphical lasso (D-S_GL) with global = TRUE. With many cells the five SILGGM procedures tend to agree; at a bulk-sample size they need not. The export we keep is the FDR-selected edge list (Cytoscape CSV via cytoscape_format and csv_save), not the full inferential dump.






Note 4.3: :information_source: Nonparanormal scores



Liu, Lafferty and Wasserman (Liu et al. 2009) define a nonparanormal vector by strictly increasing maps f_{g} such that Z_{g}=f_{g}(X_{g}) is multivariate Gaussian with mean zero, covariance R, and precision R^{-1}. If each f_{g} is unknown but monotone,

Z_{g}
=
\Phi^{-1}\bigl(F_{g}(X_{g})\bigr),

because F_{g}(X_{g}) is uniform and \Phi^{-1} returns a standard normal margin. Replacing F_{g} by a winsorised or shrunken empirical cdf is huge.npn() with npn.func = "truncation" or "shrinkage". Graphical lasso on those scores estimates the precision of Z, not of the raw counts. Both modes return an n\times G score matrix that SILGGM can take. Shrinkage is the default; truncation is the heavy-tail alternative. Means on this scale are not \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j} (Note 4.1).



Generative model
Observed margins are monotone images of one latent Gaussian vector. The precision that SILGGM tests is the precision of that latent vector, not of the counts.






%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TB
  subgraph plateC["c = 1, ..., n_j"]
    direction TB
    R["Correlation R"] --> Z(("Z_c"))
    Z --> f["Monotone f_g"]
    f --> X(["X_c"])
  end
  Th["Precision of Z, sparse"] --> R
  classDef param fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef latent fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef obs fill:#cbd5e1,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  class R,Th,f param
  class Z latent
  class X obs




Figure 4.3: Nonparanormal generative model: each gene margin is a monotone map of a latent Gaussian coordinate. SILGGM tests the precision of that latent vector.







Objective and the de-sparsified correction
The first step is still Equation 4.4, which is \ell_{1}-biased. The Janková–van de Geer correction (Jankova and Geer 2015) is not 2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}-S. On the correlation scale it is

\widehat{T}
=
2\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}
-
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}\,
\widehat{R}\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}},
\tag{4.5}
with \widehat{R} the empirical correlation. \widehat{T} recentres the edges so that they are asymptotically normal under a sparsity condition on the maximum degree. It is deliberately dense: it is an inferential object, not a generative precision. Zhang and Zou (Zhang and Zou 2014) note that graphical lasso remains useful for support recovery even when the Gaussian assumption fails. That supports edge screening, not export of \widehat{T} itself as \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}.


Optimisation and global FDR






%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone"}}%%
flowchart LR
  X["Counts"] --> N["Nonparanormal scores"]
  N --> Gl["Graphical lasso"]
  Gl --> T["Debiased T"]
  T --> FDR["Global FDR support"]
  FDR --> SPD["SPD refit"]




Figure 4.4: Estimation order for the SILGGM arm: nonparanormal scores, graphical lasso, de-sparsified matrix, global FDR support, then an SPD refit. The debiased matrix is not exported.





SILGGM runs a lasso-type fit, builds the debiased statistics, and, with global = TRUE, thresholds them by the global FDR rule for Gaussian graphical models (Liu 2013; Zhang et al. 2018a). The selected zeros define a support. An SPD precision is then refit on that support (graphical lasso constrained to the support, or a small ridge if the constrained MLE is unavailable). Edge testing and the DeCovarT precision stay separate (Equation 4.1).


Hyperparameters

npn.func: shrinkage or truncation;
method = "D-S_GL" and global = TRUE;
FDR level alpha;
lambda if it is not left at the package default;
cytoscape_format = TRUE and csv_save = TRUE only as the edge-list export.




4.3.3 Poisson-lognormal network
PLNnetwork is the sparse-precision member of PLNmodels (Chiquet et al. 2021, 2018, 2025). Fused PLN graphical lasso is a perspective (Section 4.6), not this arm.

Generative model
For each cell c in one type-time subset, with library size S_{c},

Y_{cg}\mid\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathrm{Poisson}(S_{c}Z_{cg}),
\qquad
\log\boldsymbol{Z}_{c}
\sim
\mathcal{N}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}),
\quad
\boldsymbol{\Theta}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}.
\tag{4.6}
Zeros are Poisson sampling zeros (Svensson 2020). The fit is independent for each labelled type at each of 48 h, 72 h and 96 h. A single formula with cell-type and time dummies would estimate one shared precision and only shift the mean; that is not the DeCovarT target. The formula interface is used inside each subset, with an offset and no further design.






%%{init: {"theme": "sandstone", "flowchart": {"curve": "basis"}}}%%
flowchart TB
  subgraph plateC["c in one type-time subset"]
    direction TB
    S["offset log S_c"] --> Y(["Y_c"])
    Z(("log Z_c")) --> Y
    mu["mu"] --> Z
    Sig["Sigma"] --> Z
  end
  Th["Theta = Sigma inverse, sparse"] --> Sig
  classDef param fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef latent fill:#ffffff,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  classDef obs fill:#cbd5e1,stroke:#0f172a,stroke-width:1.5px
  class mu,Sig,Th,S param
  class Z latent
  class Y obs




Figure 4.5: PLNnetwork: library size offsets a Poisson mean whose log-intensity is a sparse Gaussian. One such model per type and time.







Objective and assumptions
The observed-data likelihood integrates the latent Gaussian. That integral is intractable. Variational inference replaces the posterior of \boldsymbol{Z} by a tractable q and maximises the evidence lower bound, which is the expected complete log-likelihood minus \mathrm{KL}(q\,\|\,p(Z\mid Y)). An \ell_{1} penalty is added on off-diagonal entries of \boldsymbol{\Theta}.






Important 4.4: :information_source: Variational EM, KL, and why not Monte Carlo



EM alternates an expectation under the true conditional p(Z\mid Y) with a maximisation of the expected complete log-likelihood. When that conditional is unavailable, variational EM restricts the expectation to a family q. The identity

\log p(Y)
=
\mathrm{ELBO}(q)
+
\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q\,\|\,p(Z\mid Y)\bigr)

shows that maximising the ELBO is the same as minimising the Kullback–Leibler divergence from q to the true posterior. Equality holds when q=p(Z\mid Y), which is ordinary EM. A Monte Carlo E-step would draw the latent Gaussian at every iteration. The variational step replaces those draws by a closed-form update of q, which is why the same sparse PLN is practical at single-cell n (Chiquet et al. 2018).




Optimisation and the \ell_{1} penalty
PLNnetwork() runs that variational scheme over a grid of penalties (PLNnetwork). penalize_diagonal stays FALSE in control_main, matching the graphical-lasso convention. The penalty grid is set by penalties, or by nPenalties and min.ratio in control_init.


Hyperparameters
Inside each type-time subset the call is of the form abundance ~ 1 + offset(log_library), with log_library the natural log of that cell’s library size. Play with:

the penalty grid (penalties, or nPenalties and min.ratio);
penalize_diagonal (kept false);
outer-loop tolerances ftol_out and maxit_out only if a subset fails to converge.

Zero-inflated PLN is not the default (Note 4.5).

text:
4.4 Conclusion: twelve routes
The product in Figure 1 is

\underbrace{\{\texttt{huge},\ \texttt{SILGGM+NPN},\ \texttt{PLNnetwork}\}}_{\text{three precisions}}
\times
\underbrace{\{\text{affine},\ \text{scDesign2}\}}_{\text{two lifts}}
\times
\underbrace{\{\mathcal{G}_{0},\ \text{optional NSGA-II}\}}_{\text{two panels}}.
\tag{4.7}
Every core method must finally export

\bigl\{
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j},\,
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}
\bigr\}_{j=1}^{J},
\qquad
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j}
=
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}^{-1}
\succ 0,
\tag{4.8}
on the linear scale of Equation 4.2, not on NPN scores.



Table 4.1: Three core precision estimators.












Estimator
Reference
What it estimates
Pros
Cons




huge
Friedman et al. (2008); Zhao et al. (2012)
Sparse Gaussian \boldsymbol{\Theta}
Fast path; EBIC / StARS; maintained
Needs Gaussian rows; no library-size layer


SILGGM D-S_GL
Zhang et al. (2018a); Liu (2013)
Debiased edges, then an FDR support
Global FDR; large n makes modes agree
Debiased \widehat{T} is dense; NPN changes the mean


PLNnetwork
Chiquet et al. (2021)
Latent precision of a PLN
Counts and offset; variational, not MCMC
Heavier than graphical lasso; no edgewise FDR






The knobs that the penalty figures in Section 4.5 are meant to set are \lambda (huge), alpha (SILGGM), and the PLN penalty grid.






Warning 4.5: :warning: Why we drop zero-inflated directed graphs in the core



Directed zero-inflated DAGs are the wrong object for DeCovarT: the output is a DAG, not an undirected SPD precision. Suppinger is droplet UMI data. Svensson showed that zeros in droplet scRNA-seq are often explained by ordinary molecule-sampling counts (Svensson 2020). Keep hurdle or ZINB graphs in Section 10.1 if the observation model is to be contaminated, not as a GRN estimator.

text:
4.5 Choosing the penalty
Four displays, and only these, are used to pick the penalty for each of the three estimators. Partial-correlation weights matter, so heatmaps show the precision, not a binary adjacency.

Regularisation paths. Plot each off-diagonal entry of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}(\lambda) against \lambda or \log\lambda. This is the classical lasso path: which edges enter as the penalty relaxes.
EBIC against \lambda. Plot \mathrm{EBIC}_{\gamma}(\lambda) against \log\lambda, with a line at the minimiser (Foygel and Drton 2010). Overlay \gamma\in\{0,0.25,0.5\} when that hyperparameter is free. A flat valley means many penalties are equivalent.
Precision heatmaps along the path. At a few \lambda values, including the selected one, show


\rho_{gg'\mid\mathrm{rest}}
=
-\frac{\theta_{gg'}}{\sqrt{\theta_{gg}\theta_{g'g'}}}.
\tag{4.9}
Freeze the gene order (cluster once). Blocks that survive a stronger penalty are the stable ones. 4. Edge-count against EBIC. Put the number of edges on the horizontal axis and EBIC on the vertical axis, and mark the optimum. That is the sparsity–fit tradeoff without depending on the numerical scale of \lambda.
For SILGGM, repeat the same four pictures with the FDR level in place of \lambda when a path of alpha is computed. For PLNnetwork, the horizontal axis is the penalty grid.

text:
4.6 Perspectives

4.6.1 Cartesian GmGM cannot separate within-cell edges
GmGM replaces independent cells by a Cartesian product: gene g in cell c may depend on other genes in the same cell, or on the same gene in other cells, but not on an arbitrary pair (c,g)\neq(c',g') (Andrew et al. 2026). The precision of the vectorised matrix is a Kronecker sum of a gene precision and a cell precision. That sum forbids the cross terms that would distinguish regulation inside a cell from dependence across cells.
A strong-product Gaussian graphical model is the extension that can carry both within-cell and across-cell edges. It is not available as a drop-in for this design. Figure 4.6 sketches why labelled types still do not rescue the Cartesian support: hard cell-type blocks remove cross-type edges, but inside a type the Cartesian sum still cannot separate intracellular regulation from cell–cell dependence.






Figure 4.6: Cartesian GmGM, type-specific fits, and the strong-product extension that would separate within-cell edges from across-cell edges.





4.6.2 Sparse plus low-rank precisions
Unmeasured programmes can make the marginal precision dense. Chandrasekaran, Parrilo and Willsky split it into a sparse conditional graph minus a low-rank factor term (Chandrasekaran et al. 2012),

\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{marg}}
=
\boldsymbol{\Theta}_{\mathrm{sparse}}
-
\boldsymbol{L},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{L}\succeq 0.
\tag{4.10}
A useful reading of \boldsymbol{L} is a small set of transcription factors, or of co-regulated pathways, that lower the rank of the residual dependence. \boldsymbol{L} is a nuisance for DeCovarT, not a type covariance. This check is not in the 3\times 2\times 2 product.


4.6.3 Fused graphical lasso on a PLN
Related types can share part of a graph. The joint graphical lasso (Danaher et al. 2012) penalises both sparsity and the gap between \theta_{gg'}^{(j)} and \theta_{gg'}^{(\ell)}. PLNFGL puts a Poisson-lognormal sampling layer under that fused penalty (Zhai et al. 2026). Fusion can shrink away the rewiring DeCovarT is meant to keep, so it stays out of the independent-type comparison.


4.6.4 Other copula joints
JGCGM learns shared and subgroup-specific edges under a Gaussian copula and warns against a naive nonparanormal map on counts (Wu et al. 2020). It does not replace PLNnetwork on UMI counts. Structured penalties from earlier Chiquet work (Chiquet et al. 2012) could encode pathway modules; they are optional regularisers, not a fourth core estimator.

DeCovarT does not ingest single-cell profiles. It needs, for each labelled type j, a population-level Gaussian (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) whose precision is sparse. Affine invariance / convolution — closed-form means and covariances when cells of one type are independent Gaussians.
Optimal transport — maps and distances when we do not want to assume that the empirical cloud is already that Gaussian, including discrete (count) OT and Bures / Wasserstein-robust covariance.

title: 5  From single cells to type-level Gaussians
section: 5.2 Two aggregations that must not be confused
text:
5.2 Two aggregations that must not be confused
Write \boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j} for the expression vector of cell c in type j, and n_{j} for the number of such cells.
Type-level (population) pseudo-bulk — the object of this chapter —

\widetilde{\boldsymbol{x}}_{\cdot j}
=
\sum_{c\in C_{j}} w_{c}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j},
\qquad
\sum_{c}w_{c}=1
\ \text{or}\
w_{c}\equiv 1,
\tag{5.1}
is a weighted sum within one type. If the cells are independent, means add and covariances add (with w_{c}^{2}). This is the aggregation that estimates \boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j} and \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}.
Total bulk — the DeCovarT observation —

\boldsymbol{y}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{J} p_{j}\,\boldsymbol{x}_{\cdot j}^{\mathrm{pop}}
\tag{5.2}
is a convolution across types, with simplex weights \boldsymbol{p}. Independence across types gives \mathrm{Cov}(\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}, which is the article’s likelihood. That p_{j}^{2} is not the same calculation as Equation 5.1.
The first pipeline described “sum the cells, \Sigma scales by n, zeros of \Theta are preserved” as if it applied to whatever one calls a pseudo-bulk. The improved pipeline corrected the algebra but still risked being read as a statement about total bulk \boldsymbol{y}. Here we only aggregate within type. Convolution across types is DeCovarT’s problem, not the GRN’s.






Important 5.1: :information_source: We align cells to type-level laws, not to \boldsymbol{y}



Alignment, Wasserstein distances, and bootstrap in this chapter compare

\{\boldsymbol{x}_{c\cdot j}\}_{c\in C_{j}}
\quad\text{with}\quad
\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}).

They do not transport single cells onto a mixed bulk, and they do not estimate \boldsymbol{p}. DecOT (Section 5.4.1) is a bulk deconvolution method that uses Wasserstein loss against a reference; that is a sibling of DeCovarT, not a way to build \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}.

text:
5.5 Bootstrap and Monte Carlo

5.5.1 Technical bootstrap (available)
Resample cells with replacement within type, labels fixed. Each replicate yields (\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}^{\ast},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}^{\ast}) and therefore:

edge-inclusion frequencies (Section 6.2);
a cloud of SPD covariances whose Bures barycentre is a candidate export;
Monte Carlo error for MixSim overlap and for DeCovarT \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} in downstream simulations.

This is uncertainty conditional on this gastruloid experiment. It does not stand in for organoid-to-organoid variability (Squair et al. 2021). Calling technical pseudo-bulks “biological replicates” is the error already flagged in Note 3.4.


5.5.2 Biological bootstrap (unavailable)
Multiple donors or organoids would allow resampling experimental units. Suppinger does not. External cohorts (e.g. GSE250136) are for validation, not for pooling into one \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} without a batch model.


5.5.3 Monte Carlo from generative models
When we need more type-level profiles than n_{j} cells, or a known skeleton for BEELINE-style AUPRC, we simulate.
scDesign2 (Sun et al. 2021) fits, per cell type, a copula: a count marginal (Poisson, NB, ZIP, or ZINB, chosen per gene) plus a Gaussian copula for dependence (Theorem 5.1). It preserves genes, captures correlations, and can vary cell number and depth. It is transparent (parameters are means, dispersions, copula correlations). For our purpose: fit the copula on the GGM / PLN skeleton (constrain or initialise the copula correlation from \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}), draw synthetic cells, re-aggregate, and measure how well \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} is recovered. Using ZINB marginals should be a sensitivity, not the default, for the same reason as Note 4.5.

Theorem 5.1 (Sklar’s theorem) Let F be a G-dimensional cdf with margins F_{1},\ldots,F_{G}. There exists a copula C:[0,1]^{G}\to[0,1] such that

F(x_{1},\ldots,x_{G})
=
C\bigl(F_{1}(x_{1}),\ldots,F_{G}(x_{G})\bigr).
\tag{5.11}
If every F_{g} is continuous, C is unique. If some margins are discrete, C is uniquely determined only on \operatorname{ran}(F_{1})\times\cdots\times\operatorname{ran}(F_{G}), the Cartesian product of the ranges of the marginal cdfs (Wikipedia: Sklar’s theorem).







Note 5.2: :information_source: Discrete margins: uniqueness fails, so we jitter



The Gaussian copula takes C_{\Theta} to be the cdf of a G-dimensional standard normal with correlation (or precision) \boldsymbol{\Theta} after applying \Phi^{-1} to each uniform margin. That is the copula behind both huge.npn and scDesign2’s default dependence layer; the empirical copula is the rank analogue (Wikipedia: empirical copulas). Other parametric families (Clayton, Gumbel, t) change tail dependence; they are not required for the core simulator.
UMI counts y_{ig}\in\mathbb{N}_{0} are discrete, so Theorem 5.1 does not give a unique copula density. Two practical patches (Genest and Nešlehová, 2007, ASTIN Bulletin; not yet in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib, to add from Zotero before a review pass):

Jittering / randomised quantile. Draw U_{ig}\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1) independent of the data and set y_{ig}^{\ast}=y_{ig}+U_{ig}-1 or y_{ig}^{\ast}=y_{ig}-U_{ig}, then apply the probability-integral transform to obtain approximately \mathrm{Unif}(0,1) margins on which a Gaussian copula is well defined (lecture notes).
Mass-spreading copulas (bilinear / checkered extensions, Bernstein polynomial approximations) that spread the probability of each integer cell uniformly over a rectangle, without adding explicit jitter.

scDesign2 implements the copula on estimated count margins; treat jittering as the justification that a Gaussian copula on UMI tables is an approximation, not a uniqueness theorem.


scMultiSim (Li et al. 2025) is a mechanistic multi-omics simulator: GRN, chromatin, RNA velocity, spatial location, cell–cell interaction, technical noise. It can take a GRN as input and emit counts — the right tool for a known-skeleton benchmark in the spirit of BEELINE / SERGIO / dyngen. Most of its modalities (ATAC, space, velocity) are out of the core. The transcriptomic channel with a user GRN is in scope for metrics (Section 6.3). Do not fit scMultiSim’s full spatial/CCI stack merely to pad Suppinger.
What we reject as a default generator. Black-box GANs; simulators that do not preserve gene identity; using SERGIO’s random GRN as if it were gastruloid biology. The improved pipeline’s suggestion to feed the sparse GGM into scDesign2 / scMultiSim as a prior is the right benchmark design, not a way to invent biological replicates.

Default lift. Independent-type GGM or PLN \to export (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) on the linear scale, with sparsity transfer trusted only as “one \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j} per type”.
Alignment diagnostic. Bures–Wasserstein and KL between that Gaussian and a shrinkage covariance of the cells; semi-discrete OT only if we need to flag outlier cells.

title: 6  Evaluating networks without a true DAG
text:
6.1 What we are not claiming
There is no complete ground-truth GRN for murine gastruloids. Mouse TF catalogues are incomplete; ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq are not measured in the core Suppinger scRNA-seq table we use for \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}; and undirected GGM edges are not the same objects as directed TF–target arrows. Evaluation must therefore be relative (methods against each other, against perturbed data, and against partial priors), not a claim of causal recovery.
This chapter groups metrics into three families, following GRETA’s split of mechanistic / predictive / literature tasks and BEELINE’s emphasis on precision–recall against synthetic or curated graphs:
Directed causal metrics, multimodal ATAC/ChIP recovery, and perturbation forecasting are perspectives: they judge a different estimand than Equation 4.1.
BEELINE evaluated directed GRN algorithms, often on pseudotime-ordered cells, against synthetic Boolean networks and curated TF–gene graphs. GRETA evaluated multimodal (RNA+ATAC) pipelines on mechanistic perturbation tasks, predictive reconstruction of omics, and literature databases. Our core graphs are undirected, stationary, and transcriptomics-only. We therefore:

text:
6.2 Statistical robustness and alignment
These scores do not need a true graph. They ask whether (\widehat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_{\cdot j},\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}) is a stable, distinguishable plug-in for Equation 4.2.

6.2.1 Resampling and noise
With one experiment, the honest uncertainty is conditional on this atlas:

Technical cell bootstrap within type, labels fixed (Section 5.5). Re-estimate \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}; record edge inclusion frequencies (stability selection in the sense of Meinshausen and Bühlmann (Meinshausen and Bühlmann 2010)) and the Frobenius / Bures spread of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j}.
Gene or cell downsampling, as GRETA does to test sensitivity to coverage. GRETA found that TF and gene sets can look stable while edges collapse under downsampling — a warning we should expect for glasso supports as well.
Random seeds for stochastic estimators (GmGM, Bayesian graphs, boosting). GRETA reported that some multimodal methods reverse high-weight edges across seeds; a GGM that needs a seed should publish edge-overlap across seeds.
Observation-model contamination (Gaussian, t_{\nu}, PLN, extra zeros) belongs with Section 10.1, not as a graph-recovery score.

Biological (multi-organoid) bootstrap is unavailable. Reporting a bootstrap interval as if it were between-experiment uncertainty would repeat the pseudoreplication error of Note 3.4.


6.2.2 Likelihood and information criteria
On the Gaussian scale actually used by the estimator,

eBIC (extended BIC) is the usual glasso selection criterion when FDR methods are not used;
held-out log-likelihood on cells left out within type (still technical, not biological);
SILGGM’s own global FDR and, when a simulator supplies a true skeleton, power and Matthews correlation (the package’s simulation diagnostics).

These scores compare nested Gaussian models. They do not validate a PLN latent graph against a glasso graph on NPN data: the observation models differ. Cross-family comparison must move to a common object — the exported (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) on the linear DeCovarT scale — and use distributional distances.


6.2.3 Distances between type-level Gaussians
Closed forms, for non-degenerate P_{j}=\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}):
Kullback–Leibler

\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})
&=
\tfrac12\Bigl[
\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j})
+(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})^{\top}
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}^{-1}
(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot\ell}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})
-G
+\ln\frac{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\ell}}{\det\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}}
\Bigr].
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.1}
Jeffreys J(P_{j},P_{\ell})=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{j}\parallel P_{\ell})+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_{\ell}\parallel P_{j}) is the symmetric version used as a separation monitor in the feature chapter.
Hellinger via Gaussian affinity, and MixSim overlap \omega_{j\ell}=\Omega_{j\ell}+\Omega_{\ell j} as the sum of misclassification probabilities (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021), are the right “can DeCovarT tell these types apart?” scores. They are not graph metrics; they are metrics on the generative object.
Bures–Wasserstein (Section 5.4) splits mean displacement from covariance geometry. Use it both as a type-separation diagnostic and as an alignment loss between single-cell clouds and type-level Gaussians.






Note 6.1: :information_source: Compare laws on the DeCovarT scale



KL between NPN-space Gaussians is not KL between count-scale pseudo-bulks. After each estimator has exported Equation 4.8, compute KL / Hellinger / W_{2} / MixSim on that Gaussian, the one that enters the convolution. Otherwise a “better” SILGGM graph can win on NPN likelihood and lose as a deconvolution prior.

text:
6.3 Topological comparison

6.3.1 Skeleton scores (BEELINE, reduced to undirected)
BEELINE (Pratapa et al. 2020) is the standard scRNA-seq GRN benchmark. Its headline findings that survive our constraints:

AUPRC and early precision are moderate even with known synthetic graphs;
methods that do not require pseudotime were generally more accurate — convenient, because we assume stationarity;
recovery is easier on simple synthetic networks than on curated Boolean models.

Scores we keep, always on undirected adjacency A_{gg'}=\mathbf{1}\{\hat\theta_{gg'}\neq 0\} (or a thresholded posterior inclusion probability):








Score
Definition on skeletons
Caveat




Precision / recall / F_{1} or F_{0.1}
TP, FP, FN against a reference skeleton
Needs a reference; GRETA weights precision 10\times recall because inferred GRNs are sparse


Early precision
Precision among the top-k edges
Robust when k is the expected degree \times G/2


AUPRC / AUROC
Ranking of edges
AUROC is too optimistic on sparse graphs; prefer AUPRC


Structural Hamming distance
|A-\tilde A| on undirected edges
Scale with G; report also normalised SHD


MCC
Balanced correlation of binary edges
SILGGM simulations use it; still needs a reference



Without a true DAG, the “reference” is one of: (i) a simulator whose GRN we supplied (Section 5.5.3); (ii) another estimator (stability / concordance, not accuracy); (iii) a literature skeleton (Section 6.4). Concordance between SILGGM and PLNnetwork is a robustness number, not a validation.
CPDAG / orientation metrics from the causal-metrics notes apply only if we leave the core and score a DAG. We do not.


6.3.2 Graph summaries that do not need a reference
These describe shape, not correctness:

degree distribution and a power-law diagnostic (SILGGM used \log–\log degree plots as a biological sanity check; many biological networks are not strictly scale-free);
hub overlap across types (rewiring of hubs is a DeCovarT-relevant summary);
clustering coefficient, number of connected components, modularity;
overlap coefficients of edge sets between methods, as in GRETA (intersection over the smaller set), which avoids punishing a method for returning a larger graph.

GRETA’s most uncomfortable topological result should be treated as a prior: edge-level overlap across methods is tiny even when TF and gene sets overlap moderately. If our four core estimators disagree on edges, that is the expected state of GRN inference, not a bug unique to gastruloids. Downstream DeCovarT should therefore not depend on a single edge being true; it should depend on the SPD covariance being a stable discriminator.


6.3.3 Visualisations
The aim is to compare structure and inference, not to decorate a methods section. Each display should answer one question.
Supports and concordance

Binary adjacency heatmaps, genes ordered by a common hierarchical clustering (from a consensus distance d_{ab}=1-\bar r_{ab} of methods, or from a biological ordering). Side-by-side heatmaps of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j} for two types make rewiring visible; a third panel of |\hat\theta^{(j)}_{gg'}-\hat\theta^{(\ell)}_{gg'}| is the differential-network view.
Upset plots or Jaccard heatmaps of edge sets across the four core methods.
On-diagonal degree bars or a simple graph drawing only for a tiny TF subgraph; whole-transcriptome hairballs are not figures.

Signed partial correlations

Diverging tiles of partial correlations -\theta_{gg'}/\sqrt{\theta_{gg}\theta_{g'g'}} with a midpoint scale, not viridis (the latter encodes magnitude, not sign). Keep gene order shared across types.

Stability

Edge-inclusion frequencies from the technical bootstrap as a heatmap or as a reliability curve (precision among edges with inclusion >t, as t varies).
Sankey or alluvial only when nodes have a natural order (time, lineage). For unordered type-to-type edge flow, a chord diagram is the usual display; we do not need one in the core stationary analysis.

Distributional alignment (ties into Section 5.1)

PCA / UMAP of cells with the type-level Gaussian as an ellipse is a cartoon (UMAP is not a Gaussian space). Prefer plots of W_{2} or KL against bootstrap replicates, or rainclouds of \hat p from DeCovarT under each GRN method (package helpers plot_mc_raincloud(), plot_mc_forest()), once simulations exist.

GRETA-style genome tracks (TF–CRE–gene) require ATAC and are perspective-only (Section 6.5).

title: 6  Evaluating networks without a true DAG
text:
6.4 Knowledge-driven scoring

6.4.1 GRETA’s three buckets, restricted to undirected transcriptomics
GRETA (Badia-i-Mompel et al. 2025) modularises multimodal GRN pipelines and scores them as mechanistic, predictive, and literature-based. Core carry-over:
Literature / knowledge

Marker TFs: is a known type marker present as a hub, or as a high-degree node in \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Theta}}_{j} for that type?
TF–target edges: if g is a TF and g' a curated target, does the undirected edge \{g,g'\} appear? This is GRETA’s “known interaction” idea with orientation dropped. Resources: CollecTRI, DoRothEA, and mouse TF catalogues — all incomplete.
TF–TF via shared targets: two TFs that share many neighbours may reflect a complex or an artefact of co-expression; report overlap with PPI / IntAct only as a soft score.
TF-binding / CRE / eQTL recovery: GRETA’s ChIP-Atlas, ReMap, ENCODE, eQTL tasks need sequence assays we do not use in the core.

Predictive (observational)

How well does the graph topology predict held-out expression (gene \sim neighbours), as in GRETA’s “Omics” scores? For a GGM this is almost circular (the model is a prediction of each node given the rest), but a held-out cell nodewise R^{2} is still a useful calibration: a graph that does not predict expression of its own nodes is a bad Gaussian.
Gene-set enrichment of modules (Hallmark, KEGG, Reactome) is a sanity check, not a causal test.

Mechanistic (perturbation) — perspective. GRETA found that multimodal GRNs struggle to capture causal relationships from perturbation assays, even when predictive and literature scores look decent. That result should humble any claim that our undirected \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} is a regulatory mechanism. We do not have a gastruloid TF knockout atlas in the core pipeline; we therefore do not use TF-activity enrichment after perturbation as a gate for DeCovarT.
GRETA’s other operational warnings that apply unchanged: methods are sensitive to random seeds and to replacing a single pipeline step; paired versus unpaired multiome changes edges even when cell-type abundances look similar; de novo GRN inference from observational data is close to ill-posed. Our four-estimator design is a response to that ill-posedness, not a claim that one method is true.


6.4.2 Integer programmes and Boolean models
CORNETO (Rodriguez-Mier et al. 2025) reformulates knowledge-driven network inference as a joint constrained optimisation problem (LP / MILP) over prior knowledge networks: undirected PPI, signed directed signalling, or metabolic hypergraphs. It is not a GGM. As a perspective scorer, it can take our data-driven support (or a TF–target list derived from it) and ask whether a sparse subnetwork of a PKN explains the omics under flow / Steiner / CARNIVAL constraints. That tests mechanistic plausibility, not Gaussian fit. Joint multi-sample inference is CORNETO’s selling point; with one gastruloid experiment we would be back to a single-sample PKN extract.
Boolean / logical models (the BEELINE curated networks; BoolODE) are simpler mechanistic simulators: truth tables \to ODEs \to synthetic counts. They supply a known skeleton for AUPRC when we simulate (Section 5.5.3). They are not fitted to Suppinger as the DeCovarT graph. Using a Boolean model as the prior and a GGM as the data-driven proposal is a legitimate consistency check; using the Boolean model as \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} would abandon the Gaussian convolution.

title: 6  Evaluating networks without a true DAG
text:
6.5 Perspectives: regulatory omics
ChIP-seq, CUT&RUN, and ATAC-seq (or multiome) networks are closer to physical interaction than a partial correlation. GRETA exists because those assays still do not uniquely determine TF–gene edges: CRE-to-gene linking, motif scanning, and the modelling step each change the graph. If a later gastruloid multiome appears, GRETA is the evaluation harness; SCENIC+ / CellOracle / Dictys remain out of the DeCovarT input, because they return directed regulons, not SPD precisions. The honest use is: project our undirected skeleton onto TF–CRE–gene triples and score GRETA literature metrics; do not replace \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j} with a regulon adjacency.

text:
6.6 Practical scorecard for this repository
For each core estimator and each cell type j:

Robustness: bootstrap edge-inclusion; W_{2} / KL of \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{j} across bootstraps; seed overlap if stochastic.
Alignment: KL / Hellinger / W_{2} / MixSim between types (discrimination) and between the type-level Gaussian and the empirical cell cloud (Section 5.1).
Topology: pairwise skeleton overlap among the four estimators; degree / hub concordance; no hairball as a main figure.
Knowledge: fraction of curated TF–target pairs recovered as undirected edges; marker-TF degree; stated as overlap with an incomplete prior, not as accuracy.
Downstream (the score that actually matters for this project): DeCovarT deconvolution error under a fixed mixture design when \boldsymbol{\zeta} comes from each GRN method, with the misspecification sweep of Section 10.1.

Item 5 is the only metric that is identified with the paper’s estimand. Items 1–4 are supporting diagnostics. Perspectives (CORNETO, Boolean, ChIP/ATAC, GRETA mechanistic) stay out of the scorecard until the corresponding data or simulator is in data/processed/.

title: 7  All-versus-all gene panels
text:
7.1 All-versus-all refinement
The advanced stage treats \mathcal{G} as a subset selection problem on the full J-column signature. It comes after GRN inference (Section 4.4), because the second objective uses \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}. The loss is defined on all types jointly. That is the right geometry for DeCovarT: the likelihood depends on \boldsymbol{\mu}\boldsymbol{p} and on \sum_{j}p_{j}^{2}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}.
This stage is optional. The naive screen (Section 3.2) already supplies \mathcal{G}_{0}. The stricter panel is the second factor in the 3\times 2\times 2 design (Figure 1): huge, SILGGM, and PLNnetwork, two population lifts, and with/without this Pareto refinement.
Let \boldsymbol{\mu}=(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j})_{j=1}^{J}\in\mathbb{R}^{G\times J} be the mean signature. The 2-norm condition number is
\kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{X})
=
\frac{\sigma_{\max}(\boldsymbol{X})}{\sigma_{\min}(\boldsymbol{X})}.
\tag{7.1}
Large \kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}) is multicollinearity of the mean design (Gong and Szustakowski 2013; Newman et al. 2015). It does not see precision rewiring.

title: 7  All-versus-all gene panels
text:
7.2 Why mean-only \kappa is not enough
In a gastruloid continuum \kappa_{2} is intrinsically large. Two closely related types can share nearly collinear means and still differ in \boldsymbol{\Theta}_{j}. Mean-only pruning then under-represents adjacent or low-abundance states — exactly the types whose rewiring DeCovarT is meant to exploit. Use \kappa as a diagnostic, not as the sole selector.
A variance-weighted variant standardises rows by gene-wise uncertainties \tau_{g}^{2} and evaluates conditioning in the (J-1)-dimensional contrast space induced by \sum_{j}p_{j}=1 (package vignette supp-S6-feature-selection.qmd).

title: 7  All-versus-all gene panels
text:
7.3 Genetic algorithms
AutoGeneS searches subsets with a multi-objective genetic algorithm that minimises inter-population correlation while maximising centroid distance (Aliee and Theis 2021). The loss is already all-versus-all.
For this repository the planned optimiser is NSGA-II via mco::nsga2() (Mersmann et al. 2020). Encode genes as a mask in [0,1]^{|\mathcal{G}_{0}|} (thresholded to a target size). Minimise at least

\kappa_{2}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathcal{G}}) (mean geometry);
average pairwise overlap \overline{\omega} of the J Gaussians \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) (Melnykov et al. 2012, 2021).

MixSim defines pairwise overlap as the sum of the two misclassification probabilities under a Bayes / MAP rule, not as 1 minus a distance. Optional analytic surrogates — Jeffreys (symmetric KL), Chernoff / Bhattacharyya, and the Bures–Wasserstein metric on (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}) — belong on the same Pareto front. They use both means and covariances, which AutoGeneS correlation / centroid objectives do not.
Differential-network genes (Section 3.6.1) may be injected into \mathcal{G}_{0} before NSGA-II; they are candidates, not the panel.






Note 7.1: :information_source: A DeCovarT-specific third objective (proposal)



The improved pipeline proposed adding Fisher identifiability of \boldsymbol{p}: maximise the smallest eigenvalue of the mixture information I_{\mathcal{G}}(\boldsymbol{p}), or minimise its condition number. That objective is not in the literature corpus; it is a composition. Keep it as a sensitivity objective on a shortlist of non-dominated panels, not as the only fitness.


Keep several non-dominated panels. Report the whole front. With one Suppinger scRNA-seq resource, the honest statement is: the panel is fitted on this atlas and must be challenged on an external gastruloid cohort.

title: 8  Mean-based deconvolution comparators
text:
8.1 What is being compared
DeCovarT deconvolves bulk profiles with both a mean signature and a per-type covariance. The comparators in this part do not. They estimate a composition \boldsymbol{p} from a mean signature built on the same labelled single-cell reference, and they are the baseline against which a covariance model has to move the estimate.
Three second-generation algorithms are planned on GSE229386, at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h, for the standard Wnt pulse and the early pulse (Section 2.1):
Literature keys for these three methods are not yet in bibliography/REFERENCES.bib. Add them from Zotero before a review pass; do not cite them by invented keys.
None of the three returns (\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\cdot j},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{j}). They are composition estimators. Sensitivity of those compositions to a misspecified precision is the last chapter of this part (Section 10.1). The early-versus-standard reading of their output is Section 9.1.
No proportions are reported here. Scripts stay eval: false until the bulk and signature objects exist.

title: 8  Mean-based deconvolution comparators
text:
BayesPrism — a Bayesian model that treats the single-cell reference as a prior on cell-type expression and updates that prior with the bulk counts.
SCDC — a weighted non-negative least-squares ensemble that can combine more than one single-cell reference. Here there is only one reference, so the ensemble weight is not a second biological replicate.
DWLS — dampened weighted least squares, which down-weights genes whose mean expression would otherwise dominate the fit.

title: 9  Early versus standard Wnt
text:
9.1 Compositional reading
Second-generation mean-based deconvolution (BayesPrism, SCDC, DWLS; Section 8.1) on the bulk series is a compositional narrative, not DeCovarT’s covariance model. Figure 9.1 contrasts a standard Wnt pulse at 48 h with a premature pulse at 24 h, at the three bulk-matched times.
On the control-like arm, 72 h is primitive-streak enriched and 96 h shows pre-somitic mesoderm and somite progression. On the early Wnt arm, 48 h retains more naïve pluripotency, 72 h is dominated by ectopic pluripotency with a reduced primitive streak, and 96 h nearly loses pre-somitic mesoderm. Absolute abundances disagree across algorithms — weighted least squares is sensitive to collinearity among neighbouring states — so we treat direction of change (ectopic pluripotency up, primitive streak and pre-somitic mesoderm down) as the consensus, not the point estimates.
That reading is why GRNs are fit per type and per time at 48 h, 72 h and 96 h (Section 2.1): those are the slots where a bulk composition exists to confront the Gaussians. Cell line remains out of the precision model.

title: Appendix A — Separation, blankets, and boundaries
text:
A.1 Directed and undirected separation
Glasso returns an undirected graph. Growing a gene panel by neighbours is therefore not the same operation as blocking paths on a DAG.
On a DAG, d-separation uses the direction of edges. A chain is blocked by conditioning on the middle node; a collider is opened by conditioning on the collision node (or on one of its descendants). On an undirected graph, u-separation ignores direction: a path is blocked when it meets the conditioning set. Figure A.1 draws both.

title: Appendix A — Separation, blankets, and boundaries
text:
A.2 Blanket versus boundary
A Markov blanket of a variable X is any set S that renders X conditionally independent of the remaining variables (Pearl 1988). The neighbours of X in some undirected graph that is an I-map are always a blanket, but that graph may contain redundant edges, so the neighbour set need not be minimal.
A Markov boundary is a minimal Markov blanket. For a positive distribution, that boundary is unique and equals the neighbour set of X in the minimal undirected I-map (Pearl 1988; Koller and Friedman 2009). The boundary is therefore the lower bound on the size of a blanket: every blanket contains a boundary, and the boundary is the smallest one (Figure A.1, panel C).
In this book, Markov-boundary expansion of marker seeds (Section 3.6) means the neighbour set of a fitted undirected GGM, under the extra assumption that the fitted graph is treated as a minimal I-map. It does not mean d-separation on a regulatory DAG.
